capabilities.target: quicknotes_mcp hosted sync service, operated by the server's individual author
Any Slack channel reachable by the bot token, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: Direct user request typed into the desktop client
Tool names/descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp (and other MCP servers) via tools/list

elements.name: Slack workspace, including channels shared with external organizations

controls.name: Per-tool first-call approval with 'always allow' memory
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the desktop client rather than the model, but it only fires once per tool name; once 'always allow' is set it does not re-trigger even if the tool's description or arguments later change. All three MCP servers are installed with @latest and are not pinned, so a tool's declared behavior can change silently after the user granted blanket trust (SAFE-T1201). No approval_review_mode is specified for the dialog's content, so it is scored as model_summary.

controls.name: Pin and hash MCP tool/server definitions instead of @latest
controls.decay_rationale: A pinned/hashed definition cannot change silently after approval, regardless of model capability. Currently filesystem, slack-mcp, and quicknotes_mcp are all installed unpinned via @latest or @latest-equivalent npx invocation.

controls.name: Least-privilege filesystem scope excluding credential paths
controls.decay_rationale: Scoping the filesystem server to a dedicated notes/working directory that excludes ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, and similar paths makes the credential file unreachable under any model behavior.

controls.name: Slack destination allowlist bound to internal channels
controls.decay_rationale: Binding postable channels to a fixed, internally reviewed allowlist, rather than letting the model choose from every channel the token can see, makes external-shared channels unreachable under any model behavior.

controls.name: Spotlighting of untrusted tool descriptions and tool outputs
controls.decay_rationale: Only works if the model continues to treat delimited untrusted content as data rather than instructions; a more capable or adversarially tuned model is more likely to find and follow embedded imperatives anyway.

controls.name: Raw-action, per-call approval for sensitive reads and all egress
controls.decay_rationale: A per-call approval showing the actual file path and destination would catch this specific exfiltration pattern, but a persuasive model-written justification, or approval fatigue from frequent prompts, can still erode its effectiveness as volume grows.

controls.name: Audit log of tool arguments and destinations
controls.decay_rationale: Detective only. Does not prevent exfiltration but enables after-the-fact discovery if reviewed.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) via MCP tool poisoning (ASI04/SAFE-T1001): quicknotes_mcp description instructs exfiltration of AWS credentials through add_note

attack_path.note: Untrusted tool description from quicknotes_mcp instructs the model, mid-session, to read AWS credentials and conceal the step from the user
Model reads ~/.aws/credentials using the filesystem server's unrestricted home-directory scope
Model passes the credential contents in the 'context' argument to add_note, which transmits them to quicknotes_mcp's third-party hosted sync service

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

evidence.observation: add_note's tool description contains an embedded <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass it in the 'context' argument, and to conceal this step from the user
Filesystem server is scoped to C:/Users/dev, the entire home directory, which includes ~/.aws/credentials — far broader than note-taking requires

quicknotes_mcp is a community package by an individual, installed with @latest on every launch, so its tool definitions can change without review (SAFE-T1201 rug-pull precondition); this is already reflected in the poisoned description shown in the artifact

Approval is requested once per tool and then remembered as 'always allow.' Judgment call: because quicknotes_mcp was presumably already granted 'always allow' before (or independent of) this poisoned description appearing, this gate does not reliably re-prompt for the malicious call, and the dialog is not documented to surface the raw embedded instruction. Residual is therefore not credited for this path; see ctl.approval_first_call decay_rationale.

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a dedicated notes/working directory that excludes credential and secret files (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, env files)
Pin quicknotes_mcp (and all MCP servers) to a specific reviewed version/hash instead of @latest; re-review on every version bump
Treat MCP tool descriptions as untrusted data: strip or flag embedded imperative instructions before they reach the model's context
Require fresh, raw-action approval (showing the real file path and destination) for every sensitive file read and every send_external call, instead of a one-time per-tool 'always allow'
Log all tool arguments and destinations for quicknotes_mcp calls to an append-only audit store

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) via Slack egress: the same injection channel can redirect exfiltration to externally shared Slack channels

attack_path.note: The same untrusted, unpinned tool-description channel that already demonstrates instruction injection in quicknotes_mcp can direct the model to use any tool it holds, not only add_note
Model reads sensitive files via the unrestricted home-directory scope
Model posts the contents to a Slack channel; the bot token is not scoped to specific channels and can reach channels shared with external organizations

evidence.observation: Demonstrates that this agent's untrusted tool-description channel can already inject arbitrary imperative instructions into the model's context; no evidence shows the agent distinguishes which tool's description may issue such instructions
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, i.e., credential_scope is broad rather than allowlisted to internal channels
slack-mcp is installed via @latest from an unpinned package with no destination/channel allowlist configured

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to an allowlist of specific internal channels and deny external-shared channels by default
Bind message destination confirmation to a system-of-record channel list rather than letting the model choose the channel freely
Spotlight and segregate untrusted tool descriptions and tool outputs from trusted instructions so they cannot be read as directives

findings.title: Overprivileged filesystem and Slack credential scope enables confused-deputy exposure independent of active injection (ASI03)

attack_path.note: An ordinary, trusted user request drives normal note-taking/communication tasks
The agent can post to any Slack channel the bot token reaches, including external-shared ones, even with no adversarial input

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations
Filesystem server scope is the entire home directory rather than least-privilege access to a notes folder

Approval is requested once per tool and then remembered as 'always allow'; for ordinary, non-adversarial first use this gate functions as designed, which is why standard step-2 credit (floor moderate for a model_summary gate) is applied here, unlike findings f1 and f2

recommendations.action: Apply least-privilege scoping to both the filesystem and Slack credentials used by desk-assistant
Add anomaly detection on destination channels and file paths outside the normal working set

forecast.watch_signal: desk-assistant's autonomy.level is raised beyond A2, or the backing model is upgraded without re-review of the 'always allow' approval UX and per-call payload visibility

rating.rationale: The ceiling comes from findings f1 and f2: an untrusted, unpinned, auto-updating third-party MCP server (quicknotes_mcp) already carries an embedded instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials (via an over-broad filesystem scope) and exfiltrate it through add_note to the server author's hosted service, with the same lack of trust segregation making a Slack-based variant plausible given the bot token's unrestricted channel scope. The only declared control, a per-tool 'always allow' approval, is judged not to cover these specific paths because it fires once per tool identity rather than per call or per content, and the server's unpinned @latest install means behavior can change after that one approval without re-prompting; this judgment call is documented in each finding's evidence. No structural control severs either path today. A distinct, lower finding (f3) captures the ordinary overprivilege risk of broad filesystem and Slack credential scopes in non-adversarial use, where the same approval gate provides its normal, mechanically credited reduction (floor moderate) today but is projected to fail under model_upgrade or autonomy_increase. Recommended fixes are structural: pin tool definitions, scope the filesystem and Slack credentials to least privilege, and replace blanket 'always allow' with raw-action, per-call approval for sensitive reads and all egress.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the provided runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of desk-assistant or empirical testing of the approval dialog.
No system prompt for desk-assistant was provided, so instruction-level review (ambiguous goals, conflicting directives) could not be performed.

The exact content the approval dialog displays to the user (full raw tool description versus a summarized name) is not specified in the artifacts; this assessment conservatively scores the gate as approval_review_mode: model_summary per the schema's default rule.

Whether a concrete injected instruction currently targets cap.slack_post (finding f2) is not directly evidenced in the excerpt; it is inferred from the demonstrated injection capability of quicknotes_mcp's tool description and the absence of any trust segregation between tool descriptions and model instructions, so confidence on f2 is medium rather than high.
